# Gradiometer System with Dynamic Sensor Positioning

## System Architecture

The gradiometer system is constructed around one or more magnetic sensors that are operatively coupled to an actuation module. This actuation module serves the critical function of dynamically varying the spatial position of each sensor over time, effectively enabling a single physical sensor (or a limited set of sensors) to sample the magnetic field at multiple distinct locations throughout the course of a measurement. This approach offers significant advantages over traditional multi-sensor gradiometer designs, as it can reduce the number of physical sensors required while maintaining or enhancing gradient measurement capabilities.

## Displacement Function Governing Sensor Motion

The movement of the sensing positions is not arbitrary but is instead governed by a predetermined displacement function. This function mathematically defines the spatial displacement between different sensing positions as an explicit function of time. By establishing this displacement function in advance, the system ensures that the sensor's trajectory is well-characterized and repeatable, which is essential for the subsequent signal processing steps. The displacement function may take various forms depending on the application—including periodic (e.g., sinusoidal or triangular) waveforms, linear sweeps, or more complex trajectories—selected to optimize the gradient extraction process for particular measurement scenarios.

## Data Acquisition via the Controller

A controller within the system is responsible for acquiring readout data from the magnetic sensor(s). This readout data captures the magnetic field values sensed at each of the varying positions as the sensor moves according to the displacement function. The acquisition occurs over a specific measurement time duration, which is selected to encompass a sufficient number of position variations to enable meaningful differential and gradient calculations. The controller thus builds up a time-resolved record of magnetic field measurements corresponding to the full range of sensor positions traversed during the measurement window.

## Computation of the Differential Magnetic Field Profile

Once the readout data has been acquired, the controller processes this information to compute a differential magnetic field time profile. This profile represents the difference in magnetic field values sensed between at least two distinct sensor positions, as sampled over time. Because the sensor position changes continuously (or in discrete steps) according to the displacement function, this differential profile effectively encodes spatial magnetic field variation information, even though it is generated by what may be a single physical sensor rather than a spatially distributed array.

## Demodulation to Extract Gradient Information

The final and most critical processing step involves demodulating the differential magnetic field time profile using the same displacement function that governed the sensor's motion. This demodulation process is essential because it correlates the temporal variations in the differential signal with the corresponding spatial displacements, thereby disentangling the spatial gradient information from the temporal dynamics introduced by the sensor's movement. 

The output of this demodulation step is a demodulated time profile that directly indicates at least one vector component of the magnetic field gradient. In this way, the system effectively transforms the raw, time-varying differential signal—produced by a moving sensor—into a meaningful representation of the spatial gradient of the magnetic field, achieving the core functional objective of a gradiometer while leveraging the benefits of a dynamic, actuated sensing architecture.

# Gradiometer System with Actuated Position Modulation

## Background

Magnetic gradiometry—the measurement of spatial variations in magnetic field—plays a critical role across numerous applications including geophysical surveying, mineral exploration, unexploded ordnance detection, navigation, biomagnetic sensing, and fundamental physics research. Traditional gradiometer designs rely on arrays of two or more spatially separated magnetic sensors, with the gradient computed as the difference in field readings divided by the physical baseline distance between sensors. While effective, this conventional approach introduces significant practical challenges: sensor-to-sensor calibration mismatches, increased size and weight from multiple sensor heads, higher power consumption, and manufacturing complexity associated with maintaining precise alignment and matched response characteristics across multiple discrete sensing elements.

## System Overview

The present disclosure describes a gradiometer system that overcomes these limitations by employing a single magnetic sensor (or a reduced number of sensors) whose physical position is actively modulated in space, rather than relying on multiple fixed sensors at different locations. The system comprises three primary functional components: one or more magnetic field sensors, an actuation module mechanically coupled to the sensor(s), and a controller that manages the actuation process and processes the resulting sensor data.

### Magnetic Sensors

The magnetic sensor or sensors may be implemented using any of a variety of sensing technologies, including but not limited to fluxgate magnetometers, optically pumped magnetometers, superconducting quantum interference devices (SQUIDs), magnetoresistive sensors, Hall-effect sensors, or atomic vapor cell magnetometers. The choice of sensor technology depends on the desired sensitivity, bandwidth, operating environment, and application-specific requirements. In embodiments employing multiple sensors, the actuation-based approach described herein may be combined with traditional spatial separation to further enhance gradient resolution or to enable multi-axis gradient measurements simultaneously.

### Actuation Module

The actuation module is mechanically coupled to the magnetic sensor and is configured to periodically displace the sensor's physical position according to a predetermined displacement function. This displacement function may take various forms, including sinusoidal oscillation, triangular or sawtooth waveforms, stepwise discrete displacement, or more complex periodic trajectories tailored to specific measurement objectives. The actuation module may employ piezoelectric actuators, voice coil motors, MEMS-based actuation mechanisms, or other precision positioning technologies capable of achieving the required displacement amplitude, frequency, and positional accuracy.

The displacement function is designed to move the sensor between two or more distinct sensing positions within a defined spatial region. The amplitude of displacement—that is, the effective baseline between sensing positions—can be selected based on the spatial scale of the magnetic field gradients of interest, and may be adjustable in some embodiments to enable measurement of gradients across multiple spatial scales using the same physical hardware.

### Controller and Data Acquisition

A controller is operatively coupled to both the actuation module and the magnetic sensor(s). The controller performs several key functions:

1. **Actuation Control**: The controller generates or supplies the control signals that drive the actuation module according to the predetermined displacement function, ensuring precise and repeatable positioning of the sensor over time.

2. **Synchronized Readout**: As the sensor moves through its displacement cycle, the controller records the magnetic field readout data at a sampling rate sufficient to resolve the sensor's position throughout the displacement function. This synchronization between actuation and readout is essential for accurate signal processing.

3. **Data Storage and Buffering**: Readout data is collected and stored over a defined measurement period, which may span multiple cycles of the displacement function to improve signal-to-noise ratio through averaging or integration.

## Signal Processing and Gradient Extraction

The core innovation of this system lies in its signal processing methodology, which extracts gradient information from the time-varying signal produced by a sensor moving through a spatially varying magnetic field—without requiring physically separate sensors at each measurement position.

### Differential Field Computation

As the magnetic sensor is displaced according to the known displacement function, it samples the magnetic field at different spatial locations at different points in time. Because the displacement function is known precisely (via the actuation control signals or independent position feedback), the controller can identify which readout samples correspond to which relative sensor positions. By computing the difference between field measurements taken at different points along the displacement trajectory, the system effectively synthesizes a differential magnetic field measurement analogous to that obtained from spatially separated sensors—but using only a single physical sensing element.

### Demodulation Technique

To extract the gradient signal robustly from the continuous readout stream, the system employs a demodulation technique referencing the known displacement function. This is analogous to lock-in amplification techniques used in other precision measurement contexts: the raw sensor output, which contains a time-varying component corresponding to the sensor's motion through the field gradient, is multiplied by (or otherwise processed against) a reference signal derived from the displacement function itself. This demodulation process serves multiple purposes:

- **Noise Rejection**: By demodulating at the specific frequency (or frequencies) of the displacement function, the system rejects noise and interference at other frequencies, substantially improving the signal-to-noise ratio of the gradient measurement.

- **Signal Isolation**: The demodulation isolates the component of the sensor signal that arises specifically from spatial displacement, as distinct from temporal variations in the ambient field that would affect the sensor regardless of its position.

- **Amplitude and Phase Extraction**: The demodulated signal yields both the amplitude and phase of the gradient-induced signal component, which directly relates to the magnitude and directionality of the local field gradient.

### Vector Component Determination

By appropriately configuring the actuation module to move the sensor along multiple axes—either sequentially or through more complex multi-dimensional displacement trajectories—the system can determine multiple vector components of the magnetic field gradient tensor. For instance, displacement along the x, y, and z axes (whether through separate measurement phases or through a combined multi-axis displacement pattern) enables reconstruction of the full gradient tensor, providing comprehensive spatial derivative information about the magnetic field in the sensor's vicinity.

## Advantages

This actuation-based gradiometer architecture offers several significant advantages over conventional multi-sensor gradiometer designs:

- **Reduced Sensor Count**: By using a single sensor (or fewer sensors than would otherwise be required) to synthesize spatial gradient measurements, the system reduces hardware complexity, cost, size, and weight.

- **Elimination of Inter-Sensor Calibration**: Because measurements at different "virtual" sensor positions are obtained from the same physical sensing element, discrepancies arising from sensor-to-sensor manufacturing variation, drift, and calibration mismatch are inherently eliminated.

- **Flexible Baseline Configuration**: The effective measurement baseline can potentially be adjusted electronically or mechanically by modifying the displacement function, offering flexibility not easily achieved with fixed physical sensor separations.

- **Enhanced Noise Performance**: The demodulation approach provides inherent noise rejection benefits similar to those achieved in lock-in detection schemes, improving overall measurement sensitivity.

## Applications

This gradiometer system is well-suited to a wide range of applications requiring precise magnetic gradient measurements, including geological surveying and mineral exploration, unexploded ordnance and buried object detection, magnetic anomaly detection for navigation and surveillance purposes, biomagnetic field measurement in medical diagnostics, and fundamental physics experiments requiring high-precision magnetic field gradient characterization.

# The Word "The"

"The" is the most commonly used word in the English language, appearing more frequently than any other word in written and spoken communication. Despite—or perhaps because of—its simplicity, "the" plays a crucial grammatical role as the definite article.

## What Makes "The" Special

Unlike "a" or "an," which introduce something new or unspecified, "the" signals that the speaker and listener share a common understanding of what is being referenced. Consider the difference between:

- "I saw **a** dog in the park." (any dog, unspecified)
- "I saw **the** dog in the park." (a specific dog we both know about)

This small distinction carries significant weight in communication, helping us track what has already been introduced into a conversation versus what is new information.

## Historical Origins

The word "the" evolved from Old English, tracing back to demonstrative pronouns like "þe," "þæt," and "seo," which were gender-specific forms meaning "that" or "this." Over centuries, English simplified these variations into the single, gender-neutral word we use today.

## The Challenge for Language Learners

For non-native English speakers, "the" often proves surprisingly difficult to master. Many languages—including Russian, Japanese, and Mandarin—don't have articles at all, making the concept of definiteness expressed through a separate word entirely foreign. Even languages that do have articles may use them in different contexts than English does.

## A Word That Disappears in Plain Sight

Perhaps what's most fascinating about "the" is how invisible it becomes in everyday use. We rarely notice it, yet remove it from a sentence and something feels distinctly wrong: "Cat sat on mat" reads like a headline or a foreigner's rough translation, while "The cat sat on the mat" flows naturally. This tiny three-letter word, often overlooked, quietly holds our sentences together.

# Patent Abstract

**GRADIOMETER SYSTEM WITH MOVING MAGNETIC SENSOR AND SYNCHRONOUS DEMODULATION**

A gradiometer system and method for measuring magnetic field gradients using a moving-sensor architecture with synchronous demodulation are disclosed. The system comprises one or more magnetic field sensors mechanically coupled to an actuation module configured to displace the sensors according to a predetermined displacement function, such as a periodic, oscillatory, or reciprocating motion pattern having a known frequency, amplitude, and phase. As the sensor traverses a spatial region containing a magnetic field of interest, the sensor's periodic motion through the field gradient induces an amplitude-modulated signal component at the fundamental frequency (and/or harmonics) of the displacement function, superimposed on the baseline magnetic field signal and any static or slowly-varying noise sources. A processing module receives the sensor output signal and applies a demodulation operation—referencing the known displacement function or a derived reference signal—to extract the modulated component correlated with the sensor's spatial motion. The demodulated signal is processed to compute the magnetic field gradient at the sensor location without requiring two spatially-separated fixed sensors, thereby reducing baseline-dependent errors, common-mode noise, and sensor-matching requirements associated with conventional fixed-baseline gradiometers. The displacement function may be selected or adaptively adjusted to optimize signal-to-noise ratio, spatial resolution, or immunity to specific interference sources. Embodiments include single-axis and multi-axis actuation, feedback control of sensor position, and integration with array-based sensor configurations to enable simultaneous measurement of multiple gradient tensor components. Applications include geophysical surveying, biomagnetic sensing, unexploded ordnance detection, and navigation.

# TECHNICAL DISCLOSURE

## Title: System and Method for Extracting Magnetic Gradient Vector Components Using Spatially Reciprocating Sensor Arrays with Differential Demodulation

---

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present disclosure relates generally to magnetic field measurement systems, and more particularly to apparatus and methods for extracting spatial gradient information from magnetic fields through controlled mechanical displacement of one or more magnetic sensors between discrete or continuous positions, combined with synchronous demodulation of the resulting differential signal to isolate individual gradient tensor components.

---

## BACKGROUND

Magnetic gradiometry is employed in applications including geophysical surveying, unexploded ordnance detection, biomagnetic sensing (e.g., magnetocardiography, magnetoencephalography), navigation, and industrial non-destructive testing. Conventional gradiometers typically rely on two or more fixed, spatially separated sensors whose outputs are subtracted to approximate the spatial derivative of the magnetic field. This approach suffers from several disadvantages:

1. **Sensor mismatch**: Fixed-position gradiometers require tight matching of gain, offset, and noise characteristics between physically distinct sensors, as any mismatch appears directly as a spurious gradient signal.
2. **Baseline fixation**: The gradient baseline (sensor separation) is fixed at fabrication time, limiting flexibility in spatial resolution versus sensitivity trade-offs.
3. **Common-mode rejection limits**: Ambient field fluctuations (e.g., from distant sources, vehicle motion, or Earth's field drift) are only partially rejected due to imperfect sensor matching.
4. **Single-axis limitation**: Extracting multiple independent gradient tensor components (∂Bx/∂x, ∂Bx/∂y, ∂By/∂z, etc.) typically requires multiple sensor pairs oriented along different axes, increasing system complexity and cost.

There exists a need for a gradiometric technique that uses a reduced number of physical sensors, achieves high common-mode rejection through use of the *same* sensor at different times/positions, and allows extraction of multiple independent gradient components through a unified signal-processing framework.

---

## SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

The invention provides a system and method wherein one or more magnetic field sensors are mechanically actuated to move between at least two spatial positions according to a known, repeatable motion profile (e.g., sinusoidal oscillation, stepped displacement, or rotational sweep). As the sensor(s) traverse this motion profile, a continuous or sampled time-series of magnetic field measurements is captured. Because the sensor position is a known function of time, the resulting field signal contains a component that varies synchronously with the motion — this component is proportional to the local spatial gradient of the magnetic field along the direction of motion.

The captured signal is processed by a demodulation stage — implemented as a lock-in amplifier, synchronous detector, or equivalent digital signal processing algorithm (e.g., Fourier component extraction, quadrature demodulation) — referenced to the known mechanical motion frequency and phase. This demodulation isolates the gradient-proportional component from the (undesired) absolute field component and from uncorrelated noise, yielding an output signal proportional to one or more components of the magnetic field gradient tensor.

By employing multiple motion axes (sequentially or simultaneously via orthogonal actuation, e.g., using a multi-axis piezoelectric or electromagnetic actuator), the system can extract multiple independent gradient tensor components using a single physical sensor element, thereby eliminating inter-sensor mismatch errors that plague conventional fixed-baseline gradiometers.

---

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION

### 1. System Architecture

Referring to the general embodiment, the system comprises:

**(a) Magnetic Sensor Element(s)**
One or more magnetic field sensors selected from: fluxgate magnetometers, magnetoresistive sensors (AMR, GMR, TMR), Hall-effect sensors, optically pumped magnetometers (OPM), SQUIDs, or search-coil magnetometers. The sensor may be a scalar (total-field) or vector sensor.

**(b) Actuation Subsystem**
A mechanical or electromechanical positioning mechanism configured to move the sensor between two or more positions along a defined axis or set of axes. Suitable actuators include:
- Piezoelectric linear/tip-tilt actuators
- Voice-coil actuators
- Rotary motors with cam or eccentric linkages
- MEMS-based micro-positioning stages
- Flexure-based resonant oscillators driven at a natural mechanical resonance for energy-efficient reciprocation

The actuation subsystem is driven by a reference oscillator or motion controller that generates a known position waveform p(t), which may be sinusoidal, triangular, square-wave (stepped), or an arbitrary periodic function.

**(c) Position/Phase Reference Generator**
A reference signal, synchronized with the actual mechanical motion (via encoder, capacitive position sensor, or the drive waveform itself with calibrated phase lag), is provided to the demodulation stage to establish the phase and frequency reference for synchronous detection.

**(d) Signal Conditioning and Digitization**
The raw sensor output is amplified, filtered (anti-alias), and digitized via an analog-to-digital converter (ADC) at a sampling rate sufficient to resolve the motion frequency and its relevant harmonics (typically ≥10× the motion frequency).

**(e) Demodulation / Extraction Module**
A digital or analog synchronous demodulator that multiplies the digitized sensor signal by reference sine/cosine waveforms at the motion frequency (and optionally harmonics), followed by low-pass filtering, to produce in-phase (I) and quadrature (Q) components. These I/Q components are mathematically related to the local gradient magnitude and phase (position-dependent sign) of the field along the motion axis.

**(f) Gradient Vector Reconstruction Module**
A computational module that combines demodulated outputs from multiple motion axes (or multiple sequential measurement passes) to reconstruct the full or partial magnetic gradient tensor, ∇B, including off-diagonal shear terms where multi-axis actuation is employed.

---

### 2. Principle of Operation

Consider a sensor undergoing position modulation along the x-axis:

```
x(t) = x₀ + A·sin(ωₘt)
```

where A is the oscillation amplitude and ωₘ is the mechanical modulation frequency.

The magnetic field at the sensor location can be expressed via a first-order Taylor expansion about the equilibrium position x₀:

```
B(x(t)) ≈ B(x₀) + (∂B/∂x)|ₓ₀ · A·sin(ωₘt) + O(A²)
```

The sensor output signal S(t) is therefore:

```
S(t) = B(x₀) + G_x · A · sin(ωₘt) + n(t)
```

where G_x = ∂B/∂x is the gradient component of interest, and n(t) represents noise and higher-order/nonlinear terms.

Demodulation at frequency ωₘ (multiplying by sin(ωₘt) and low-pass filtering) extracts:

```
I = (1/T)∫ S(t)·sin(ωₘt) dt ≈ (G_x · A)/2
```

Thus, the static (DC) component B(x₀) — which does not vary at ωₘ — is rejected by the synchronous detection process, while the term proportional to G_x, oscillating precisely at ωₘ, is preferentially extracted. This provides intrinsic **common-mode rejection of the ambient/absolute field** without requiring a second, physically distinct sensor with matched characteristics.

Extension to full-tensor recovery is achieved by:
- Sequential modulation along x, y, and z axes (time-multiplexed), or
- Simultaneous modulation along orthogonal axes at distinct frequencies ωₓ, ω_y, ω_z (frequency-multiplexed), permitting parallel extraction of ∂B/∂x, ∂B/∂y, ∂B/∂z via independent demodulation channels, or
- Circular/elliptical motion trajectories combined with multi-frequency or multi-harmonic demodulation to extract off-diagonal tensor terms (e.g., ∂Bx/∂y) when a vector sensor is used.

---

### 3. Alternative Embodiments

**Embodiment A — Single-Axis Reciprocating Sensor**
A single scalar magnetometer is oscillated linearly along one axis by a piezoelectric bimorph. Demodulation at the drive frequency yields one gradient component. Multiple sequential measurements with reoriented actuator axis yield the remaining components.

**Embodiment B — Dual-Axis Simultaneous Modulation**
A vector magnetometer is mounted on a two-axis flexure stage driven at two distinct, non-harmonically-related frequencies (e.g., ωₓ = 2π·137 Hz, ω_y = 2π·211 Hz). Simultaneous dual-frequency demodulation yields ∂B/∂x and ∂B/∂y concurrently without cross-talk, subject to frequency-selective filtering.

**Embodiment C — Rotational Sensor Sweep**
The sensor is affixed to a rotating arm of fixed radius r, sweeping through angle θ(t) = ω_r·t. The field measured at radius r as a function of θ contains Fourier components corresponding to the gradient tensor projected onto the rotation plane; harmonic demodulation (1st and 2nd harmonics of ω_r) extracts the corresponding gradient tensor components, analogous to a synthetic-aperture approach.

**Embodiment D — Stepped (Non-Continuous) Position Switching**
Rather than continuous oscillation, the sensor is switched between two discrete fixed positions at a known switching frequency using a bistable actuator (e.g., electromagnetic relay-driven stage). The resulting square-wave-modulated signal is demodulated using a matched square-wave (or its Fourier fundamental) reference, offering an implementation with simplified actuator mechanics at the cost of introducing switching-transient artifacts requiring blanking/gating in the demodulation window.

**Embodiment E — Resonant Mechanical Amplification**
The sensor/actuator assembly is designed such that the modulation frequency ωₘ coincides with a mechanical resonance of the sensor mount, amplifying the effective oscillation amplitude A for a given actuator drive power, thereby improving the signal-to-noise ratio of the extracted gradient signal without increasing electrical drive requirements.

---

### 4. Signal Processing Details

The demodulation module may be implemented as:

- **Analog lock-in amplifier**: mixer + low-pass filter implemented in analog hardware, offering low latency.
- **Digital lock-in / software-defined demodulation**: digitized samples processed via multiplication with digitally generated reference waveforms followed by digital low-pass (e.g., CIC or FIR) filtering; enables multi-frequency, multi-harmonic extraction from a single ADC data stream.
- **FFT-based bin extraction**: block-wise FFT of the sampled signal with extraction of the complex coefficient at bin(s) corresponding to ωₘ (and harmonics), offering simultaneous multi-frequency demodulation without separate mixer chains.
- **Kalman filter / adaptive notch approach**: state-space estimation of the amplitude and phase of the known-frequency component, providing improved tracking under non-stationary drive amplitude or frequency drift.

# Summary of the Invention

The present disclosure relates to a device and method for measuring magnetic field gradients through the use of a spatially oscillating sensor arrangement combined with synchronized signal processing.

## Background

Conventional magnetic gradiometers typically rely on two or more spatially separated, fixed-position sensors, with the gradient computed as a difference signal between them. Such arrangements are sensitive to manufacturing mismatches between sensors, baseline drift, and calibration errors that can introduce significant measurement inaccuracies, particularly for small gradient signals.

## Summary

In accordance with one or more embodiments, a magnetic field gradient measuring device is provided that comprises:

- **A magnetic field sensor** configured to detect a magnetic field parameter at a given location;
- **An oscillation mechanism**, operatively coupled to the sensor, configured to periodically displace the sensor between at least two spatial positions along a predetermined axis or path, such that the sensor traverses a region of space over time rather than remaining fixed;
- **A signal acquisition unit** configured to record the output of the sensor as a time-varying signal corresponding to the magnetic field sensed at each of the oscillating positions; and
- **A controller**, communicatively coupled to the oscillation mechanism and the signal acquisition unit, configured to:
  - synchronize the timing of signal acquisition with the known or measured position of the sensor during oscillation;
  - process the resulting time-varying signal to extract a spatial magnetic field gradient based on the variation of the sensed field as a function of sensor position; and
  - output a gradient measurement signal representative of the magnetic field gradient at the measurement location.

In certain embodiments, the oscillation mechanism may include a mechanical actuator, a piezoelectric transducer, an electromagnetic driver, or other suitable means for producing a periodic, repeatable displacement of the sensor. The oscillation may be sinusoidal, triangular, stepped, or otherwise periodic in nature, and may occur along a linear axis, an arc, or a more complex trajectory.

The controller may further be configured to apply one or more signal processing techniques—including but not limited to synchronous (lock-in) detection, Fourier transformation, filtering, or demodulation referenced to the oscillation frequency—in order to isolate the gradient-dependent component of the signal from noise, common-mode field variations, and other interfering signals.

By employing a single sensor that is oscillated through a range of positions, rather than multiple discrete sensors, the present device advantageously reduces or eliminates errors arising from sensor-to-sensor mismatch, enabling improved sensitivity, reduced calibration burden, and a simplified physical construction. Additional advantages, embodiments, and features are described in the detailed description that follows.

---

# Abstract

A gradiometer system and associated method for determining a magnetic field gradient are disclosed. The system comprises a plurality of magnetic field sensors arranged at known, spatially-separated locations, and a controller operably coupled to the sensors. The controller is configured to obtain sensor readout data from at least two magnetic field sensors, each readout data representing a magnetic field measurement at a respective sensor location. The controller computes a differential magnetic field profile based on a comparison of the readout data obtained from the plurality of sensors, the differential profile representing spatial variation in the magnetic field across the sensor array. The controller further demodulates the differential magnetic field profile using a known displacement function corresponding to the fixed or time-varying spatial separation between the sensors, thereby extracting a magnetic field gradient value substantially independent of common-mode noise and uniform background fields. The disclosed configuration enables improved rejection of environmental interference and enhanced sensitivity in gradient measurements, and is applicable to navigation, geophysical surveying, biomagnetic sensing, and unexploded ordnance detection applications requiring precise localization of magnetic field sources.

# INVENTION SUMMARY

## MAGNETIC GRADIOMETER SYSTEM WITH DYNAMICALLY DISPLACED SENSORS AND DEMODULATION-BASED GRADIENT EXTRACTION

### Field of the Invention

The present disclosure relates generally to systems and methods for magnetic field measurement, and more particularly to a magnetic gradiometer system in which the relative positions of a plurality of magnetic field sensors are varied in accordance with a predetermined displacement function, wherein components of a magnetic field gradient tensor are determined by demodulation of a differential magnetic field signal derived from the sensors.

### Background

Conventional magnetic gradiometers typically employ two or more magnetic field sensors maintained at a fixed baseline separation, with the gradient computed as a simple difference of the sensed field values divided by the fixed separation distance. While such static-baseline configurations are straightforward to implement, they suffer from several limitations, including sensitivity to sensor-to-sensor calibration mismatch, common-mode drift, low-frequency noise, and an inability to distinguish true spatial field gradients from temporally varying common-mode disturbances. Moreover, fixed-baseline systems provide only a single, static estimate of baseline-dependent gradient information and cannot readily extract multiple independent gradient tensor components without deploying additional sensor pairs at different fixed baselines and orientations, thereby increasing system complexity, size, weight, and power requirements. There exists a need for a gradiometer architecture capable of extracting multiple gradient tensor components using a reduced sensor complement, while providing inherent rejection of common-mode noise and drift.

### Summary of the Invention

In accordance with one or more embodiments, there is provided a magnetic gradiometer system comprising a plurality of magnetic field sensors, at least one actuator or positioning mechanism configured to impart relative displacement between the sensors, a controller configured to drive the relative sensor displacement in accordance with a predetermined, time-varying displacement function, and a signal processing subsystem configured to receive a differential magnetic field signal representative of a difference between magnetic field measurements obtained from the sensors, and to determine one or more components of a magnetic field gradient by demodulating the differential magnetic field signal using a reference signal derived from, or corresponding to, the predetermined displacement function.

In one aspect, the plurality of magnetic field sensors comprises a first magnetic field sensor and a second magnetic field sensor, and the relative displacement is imparted between the first and second sensors such that a baseline vector separating the sensors varies over time according to the predetermined displacement function. The displacement function may define a periodic, oscillatory, or otherwise time-varying trajectory, including but not limited to a sinusoidal displacement, a multi-axis displacement pattern, or a displacement pattern comprising a plurality of superposed frequency components, each frequency component being associated with a distinct spatial direction or gradient tensor component.

In another aspect, the actuator or positioning mechanism is configured to mechanically translate at least one of the sensors relative to the other along one or more axes in accordance with the displacement function. In alternative embodiments, the effective relative displacement may be produced by electronically or optically switching among, weighting, or interpolating between outputs of a fixed array of sensor elements disposed at a plurality of spatial locations, such that a synthesized effective sensor position varies over time in accordance with the predetermined displacement function without requiring physical motion of the sensor elements.

In a further aspect, the signal processing subsystem comprises a differencing circuit or difference-computation module configured to generate the differential magnetic field signal from the outputs of the plurality of sensors, and a demodulator configured to multiply, correlate, or otherwise combine the differential magnetic field signal with a reference signal corresponding to the predetermined displacement function, or to a harmonic or derivative thereof, to produce a demodulated output signal from which the gradient component is derived. The demodulator may comprise a lock-in amplifier, a synchronous detector, a mixer followed by a low-pass filter, or a digital signal processor configured to execute a corresponding demodulation algorithm.

In yet a further aspect, because the predetermined displacement function may comprise multiple distinct frequency components or multiple distinct directional components, the signal processing subsystem may be configured to demodulate the differential magnetic field signal at each of the respective frequencies or in association with each of the respective directional components, thereby extracting a plurality of independent gradient tensor components from a single differential signal obtained using a reduced number of sensors. The system may thereby determine, from the demodulated outputs, one or more elements of a magnetic field gradient tensor, including diagonal and/or off-diagonal components thereof.

In another aspect, the predetermined displacement function is selected such that a frequency, phase, or amplitude thereof lies within, or is separated from, a frequency band associated with common-mode noise, ambient field fluctuations, or sensor drift, such that demodulation of the differential signal at the frequency associated with the displacement function provides rejection of noise components not correlated with the imparted displacement, thereby improving signal-to-noise ratio and gradient measurement accuracy relative to static-baseline gradiometer configurations.

In still another aspect, the system further comprises a calibration module configured to determine or update one or more parameters of the predetermined displacement function, a scale factor relating the demodulated output signal to a gradient magnitude, or a mapping between demodulated signal components and corresponding gradient tensor elements, based at least in part on a known or reference magnetic field applied to the sensors during a calibration procedure.

In accordance with a further embodiment, there is provided a method of measuring a magnetic field gradient, comprising: displacing at least one magnetic field sensor relative to another magnetic field sensor in accordance with a predetermined displacement function; obtaining magnetic field measurements from the sensors during the displacement; generating a differential magnetic field signal based on the magnetic field measurements; demodulating the differential magnetic field signal using a reference signal associated with the predetermined displacement function; and determining, based on the demodulated differential magnetic field signal, one or more components of a magnetic field gradient.

The disclosed system and method advantageously enable extraction of multiple independent gradient components with a reduced sensor count, provide inherent common-mode noise rejection through synchronous demodulation, and permit flexible reconfiguration of the effective measurement baseline through selection or modification of the predetermined displacement function, thereby offering improved sensitivity, reduced size, weight, and power, and enhanced adaptability relative to conventional fixed-baseline gradiometer architectures.

### Brief Summary of Advantages

Embodiments of the present disclosure may provide one or more of the following advantages: (i) extraction of multiple gradient tensor components from a reduced number of physical sensors; (ii) improved rejection of common-mode and low-frequency drift noise through synchronous demodulation referenced to a known displacement function; (iii) reconfigurability of effective baseline and measurement axis through software-defined or mechanically-defined displacement functions; and (iv) compatibility with both mechanically actuated and electronically synthesized sensor displacement implementations.

---

*It will be understood that the foregoing summary is illustrative only and is not intended to limit the scope of the invention. Additional aspects, features, and embodiments will become apparent from the detailed description, drawings, and claims that follow.*
